title_guess: Capital market: government securities, zero-coupon vs coupon bonds, primary and secondary markets, bond yield
running_examples: ₹1 lakh face-value government security sold at a discount for ₹90K
face value ₹10K: zero-coupon bought at ₹9.5K gives ₹500 return; gilt-edged pays 5% coupon each year
10-year bond, 5% coupon, ₹10K face value = ₹500 a year; resold at ₹9K, ₹15K, ₹5K the yield becomes 5.5%, 3.3%, 10%

best_moments.why: the financial market as a handover: a hand marked fund surplus passes a money bundle to an open hand marked fund scarce
a cream blob traces the path from capital market down to government securities and then stays as a left-side road map whose highlight moves with the lesson
one bond certificate steps down a chain of owners; each owner pays a different price for the same fixed ₹500 and gets a different yield
the three resale prices from the story become three dots on a falling yield-vs-price curve, then the inverse formula

weak_moments.why: bond and zero-coupon bond explained in two long paragraph boxes side by side
real bank and company logos used as the bond buyers
the recap tree is hidden under an app promotion overlay

segments.teaches: the financial market moves money from those with surplus funds (lenders) to those short of funds (borrowers)

elements.what: upper hand passing a round money bundle down to an open lower hand, inside a soft circle
blue 'fund surplus / lend money' and dark 'fund scarce / borrow money' tags on the two hands
pointer label 'money' on the bundle
FINANCIAL MARKET

segments.notes: opening picture that is reused as a small badge on the next canvas
segments.idea: a financial market is where people with spare money lend it to people who need it
segments.shown_as: one hand marked fund surplus / lend passes a round money bundle down to an open hand marked fund scarce / borrow, inside a soft circle titled financial market

segments.teaches: the financial market splits into the money market (short term, up to 364 days) and the capital market (long term, more than 364 days)

elements.what: the handover picture shrunk to a badge at the top
financial market splits into money market and capital market with green elbow arrows
short-term / long-term financial market sub-labels
italic 'up to 364 days' and red 'more than 364 days'
wavy divider between the sides, then a pale blue panel over the money-market side

segments.notes: the 364-day line is the one number that separates the two markets
segments.idea: money lent for up to a year trades in the money market; longer than a year, in the capital market
segments.shown_as: the hand picture shrinks to the top; green elbow arrows split financial market into money market and capital market, separated by a wavy line; each side gets its time limit (up to 364 days vs more than 364 days, the second in red); a pale blue panel then lights up the money-market side

segments.teaches: capital market = institutional financing + securities market; securities market = government and corporate security markets, each with primary and secondary markets; long-term money is raised through shares, bonds and debentures

elements.what: capital market -> institutional financing / securities market -> government / corporate security market -> primary / secondary under each
black frame on securities market
box: long-term capital raised via shares, bonds, debentures
yellow shaded block under the securities subtree
SHARES, BONDS, DEBENTURES chips
dotted cream blob tracing only the path to the government security market

segments.notes: the blob becomes a persistent left-side navigator for the rest of the video; its framed node changes as the lesson moves (government security market, then primary, then secondary)
segments.idea: the capital market branches down to the government securities market, which has a primary and a secondary side
segments.shown_as: a fresh tree: capital market splits into institutional financing and securities market, which splits into government and corporate security markets, each splitting into primary and secondary; a black frame grabs securities market and a callout lists shares, bonds and debentures, which appear as three chips under a shaded block; finally a cream blob wraps only the path down to the government security market, marking the road the lesson will take

segments.teaches: the government issues securities through the RBI in the primary (new issue) market to banks and NBFCs, sold at a discount to face value

elements.what: national emblem (issuer) and RBI coin logo
certificate with a ribbon (security)
emblem -> certificate -> RBI, then RBI down to the market banner
blue 'PRIMARY MARKET / new issue market' banner with 'banks & NBFCs' under it
small upright token with a green tick on an up-arrow beside the down-arrow (payment going up)
'government security @ discounted price'
'face value 1 lakh' then 'discounted price 90K'

segments.notes: the capital-market tree shrinks into a left panel (road map); the right side is the working canvas from here on
segments.idea: the government sells IOUs through the RBI to banks for less than the amount it will pay back
segments.shown_as: on the right, the government emblem hands a certificate to the RBI coin (arrows emblem -> certificate -> RBI); RBI drops the certificate down an arrow into a blue primary-market banner where banks and NBFCs sit; an up-arrow with a small ticked token beside the down-arrow shows payment going up as the certificate goes down; a label says it is sold at a discount and a pointer adds face value 1 lakh, discounted price 90K

segments.teaches: government securities are long term (over 364 days); sold at a discount they are zero-coupon bonds, otherwise ordinary bonds (G-secs), also called gilt-edged securities for their top quality

elements.what: emblem + certificate group with the discount tag, moved to the top
'more than 364 days' over the group
yes/no fork: green Y to zero coupon bond, red N to bond
G-SECS chip under bond
quote chip 'of highest quality' with a curved pointer to GILT-EDGED security

segments.notes: the Y/N fork is a compact decision device (is it sold at a discount?)
segments.idea: a government bond either pays no interest and sells cheap (zero-coupon) or pays interest (G-sec, gilt-edged)
segments.shown_as: the issuer group (emblem + certificate) moves to the top with its discount tag; a yes/no fork hangs below: the green Y branch ends in zero-coupon bond, the red N branch ends in bond, tagged G-secs; a quote chip 'of highest quality' points with a curved line to a new name, gilt-edged security

segments.teaches: gilt-edged bonds pay periodic interest (coupon) and return the principal at maturity; zero-coupon bonds pay no interest, sell below face value and the gap is the return

elements.what: pale-blue definition under bond (coupon and principal) with 'coupon rate' label
longer pale-blue definition under zero-coupon bond
wavy divider; red ring around the word coupon
red tag 'interest' pointing at the ringed word

segments.idea: one kind pays you interest every year, the other pays nothing until the end but costs less
segments.shown_as: under each branch a pale-blue definition box fades in (left: pays coupon, returns principal; right: no coupon, bought below face value, the gap is your return), split by a wavy line; then the word coupon is ringed in red and a pointer tag translates it as interest

segments.teaches: worked example: both bonds have face value ₹10K; zero-coupon sells at ₹9.5K with 0% coupon so the return is ₹500; gilt-edged sells at ₹10K and pays 5% a year plus principal at the end

elements.what: 2 rows (zero coupon, gilt-edged) x 3 columns (face value, discounted price, coupon rate) filled cell by cell
black box on the 9.5K cell, later on the gilt 10K cell
return = 10K - 9.5K = 500
bracket spanning face value to price with a note; callout under 5% about yearly coupon and principal

segments.notes: the table turns the two definitions into numbers; the bracket literally spans the gap that is the return
segments.idea: with the same ₹10K face value, the zero-coupon earns by buying cheap, the gilt earns by yearly coupon
segments.shown_as: two row labels appear, then a three-column table fills cell by cell (10K and 10K face values; 9.5K vs a dash for price; 0% vs 5% coupon); the 9.5K cell gets a black box and a bracket spanning face value to price drops a note and a formula on top (10K - 9.5K = 500 return); then the gilt row's 10K is boxed and the 5% gets a callout about yearly coupon plus principal
segments.example: face value ₹10K; zero-coupon bought at ₹9.5K -> ₹500 return; gilt-edged at 5% coupon

segments.teaches: RBI issues both kinds of G-sec in the primary (new issue) market; already-issued bonds trade in the secondary market, where demand and supply set the price

elements.what: emblem + certificate over the RBI coin
RBI forks into gilt-edged security and zero coupon bond
rows of three short down-arrows into each banner
blue PRIMARY MARKET (new issue) and SECONDARY MARKET (old issues) banners
note: in the secondary market demand and supply set the price
road-map frame hops from primary to secondary on the left panel

segments.notes: left road map and right canvas move together: when the narrator says secondary, both highlight it
segments.idea: new bonds are first sold by the RBI, then the same bonds keep changing hands at market prices
segments.shown_as: emblem and certificate sit over the RBI coin, which forks into the two bond types; a rain of short down-arrows drops from both into a blue primary-market banner, and another rain falls from it into a second blue banner, the secondary market of old bonds; on the left road map the highlight frame hops from primary to secondary as the narrator moves

segments.teaches: running example: a 10-year bond with 5% coupon and ₹10K face value pays ₹500 a year; a bank buys it first in the primary market

bond terms in the band: 10 year bond, coupon 5%, face value 10K
certificate in the band
yellow tag 'interest every year 500' pinned to the certificate
a real bank's logo as first buyer

segments.notes: the empty grey boxes set up the next beat before anything moves
segments.idea: a bond's coupon is fixed in rupees: ₹500 a year on ₹10K, whoever holds it
segments.shown_as: under the RBI coin a blue band holds the bond's terms (10 years, 5% coupon, ₹10K) and the certificate; a tag pinned to the certificate says ₹500 interest every year; a bank logo appears in the band as the first buyer, and a column of three empty grey boxes linked by down-arrows waits below for later owners
segments.example: 10-year bond, 5% coupon, ₹10K face value -> ₹500 a year

segments.teaches: when the bond is resold at different prices, the fixed ₹500 gives different yields: bought at ₹9K -> 5.5%, at ₹15K -> 3.3%, at ₹5K -> 10%

elements.what: certificate moving down into grey box 1, 2, then 3, its interest tag following
two real company logos as later buyers
price paid beside each box: 9K, 15K, 5K
red 'yield = 5.5%' and 'yield = 3.3%' written next to the prices

segments.notes: same fixed coupon, different price -> different yield; BIE must use generic buyer figures, not real brands
segments.idea: pay more for a bond and its fixed interest is a smaller share of what you paid, so its yield falls
segments.shown_as: the certificate steps down the chain of grey boxes, one owner at a time, its '500 every year' tag riding along; at each stop a new buyer logo and the price paid appear beside it (9K, then 15K, then 5K) and a red yield figure is written next to the price (5.5% at 9K, 3.3% at 15K)

segments.teaches: bond yield moves inversely to bond price in the secondary market

elements.what: yield (y) vs bond price (x): falling curve with three dots and dashed drop lines at (5K, 10%), (9K, 5.5%), (15K, 3.3%)
yield proportional to 1 / bond price
panel turns pink
one-line note on the inverse relation

segments.notes: story numbers reused as graph points: a clean bridge from example to rule
segments.idea: the higher the price you pay for a bond, the lower its yield
segments.shown_as: the three resale prices become three dots on a falling curve (5K at 10%, 9K at 5.5%, 15K at 3.3%) with dashed drop-lines to both axes; the panel turns pink and the formula 'yield ∝ 1/bond price' appears, then a one-line note says yield depends on the secondary-market price
